question: Question linked to the image nº4 Woman of 65 years. Consultation for constitutional syndrome associated with progressive epigastric abdominal pain irradiated at the back, two months of evolution. The diagnosis of suspicion of adenocarcinoma of the pancreas is confirmed by biopsy guided by endoscopic ultrasound. Abdominal CT was performed after administration of intravenous contrast for evaluation of vascular structures close to the pancreatic tumor, in order to establish its possible affectation. (view image). What vascular structure is absent, thrombosed by tumor infiltration, conditioning collateral circulation in the gastric wall?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Tumor infiltration -> thrombosis of a vascular structure -> collateral circulation in the gastric wall -> absent vascular structure is the splenic vein -> 85% confidence. CHAIN: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma -> tumor growth -> compression of nearby vascular structures -> thrombosis of the splenic vein -> 80% confidence. CHAIN: Progressive epigastric abdominal pain -> suspicion of pancreatic adenocarcinoma -> biopsy confirmation -> absent splenic vein due to tumor infiltration -> 85%
enhanced_information: The absent vascular structure thrombosed by tumor infiltration, conditioning collateral circulation in the gastric wall is the splenic vein. Consensus supports the chain of tumor infiltration leading to thrombosis of the splenic vein, causing collateral circulation issues in the gastric wall.
analysis: The image and enhanced information point towards tumor infiltration causing thrombosis of the splenic vein, leading to collateral circulation issues in the gastric wall. This scenario is commonly seen in pancreatic adenocarcinoma. The absence of the splenic vein due to tumor infiltration is the most likely cause of the collateral circulation problem in the gastric wall.
